title: India's Refiners Were Eyeing Iranian Crude Again. Then Washington Killed the Waiver.
excerpt: Indian state-owned oil companies had been positioning for a return to Iranian oil purchases. The US revocation of sanctions waivers — and the collapse of the ceasefire — has scrambled their calculations.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US revoked sanctions waivers, halting Iranian oil sales to India.
  • India imports 85% of its crude, heavily reliant on foreign suppliers.
  • Russian oil is now cheaper than Iranian crude for Indian refiners.
  • Brent crude prices spiked to $79.76 amid geopolitical tensions.
  • Strait of Hormuz operates at 50% capacity, impacting global oil supply.

India's state-owned refiners were quietly exploring something they hadn't done in years: buying Iranian crude oil. Then Washington pulled the rug. The US Treasury Department on Tuesday revoked the temporary sanctions waiver that had allowed Iran to sell oil since mid-June, cutting off Tehran's most important revenue stream just weeks after reopening it. The move came within hours of Iran attacking three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz — and before President Trump declared the fragile ceasefire with Iran "over" at the NATO summit in Ankara. ## A Window That Opened and Slammed Shut Under the 14-point memorandum of understanding signed with Iran in June, Washington had authorized Iranian oil sales through August 21. The window was supposed to give diplomacy time to work. Indian state refiners — including Indian Oil Corporation, the country's largest — had been in preliminary talks with traders marketing Iranian crude, according to Bloomberg. They weren't rushing to buy. Indian refiners had already locked in shipments through August from non-Middle Eastern sources during the months when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. But they were positioning for the possibility that the waiver might extend past August. > **"The move came within hours of Iran attacking three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz — and before President Trump declared the fragile ceasefire with Iran "over" at the NATO summit in Ankara."** That possibility is now dead. ## The Arithmetic of Indian Oil Imports India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, making it the world's third-largest importer and consumer. The arithmetic of who India buys from has shifted dramatically since the Iran war began in February. Russia remains India's top supplier, offering Urals crude at a discount of roughly $6 per barrel to Brent. Iranian crude, by contrast, was being offered at only $4 to $5 below Brent — making Russian oil the better deal even when Iran's was technically legal to buy. Saudi Arabia has also slashed prices aggressively, recording its biggest monthly reduction in official selling prices since at least 2000, as Gulf producers compete for Asian customers whose orders had shifted to non-Middle Eastern sources during the conflict. Indian Oil Corporation this week chartered a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to load crude from Iraq — the first significant Iraqi oil shipment to India since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed by the war. The crude will be delivered to India's eastern ports of Paradip and Chennai, signalling a tentative normalisation of supply routes even as the diplomatic situation deteriorates. ## Brent at $77 and Climbing Oil prices spiked more than 7 percent on Wednesday after Trump declared the ceasefire over, with Brent crude hitting $79.76 per barrel before easing back to around $77.50 on Thursday. Goldman Sachs projects a $75 to $85 range over the coming month, with an upward bias if hostilities continue.
Impact of Oil Price Surge
›$79.76 Brent crude spiked over 7% after ceasefire declaration.
›One-month low Indian rupee dipped to 95.50 per dollar.
›Goldman Sachs projects Brent at $75-$85 range.
›Higher oil prices could strain India's current account.
For India, every dollar increase in the price of Brent widens the import bill, stokes inflation, and pressures the rupee. The Indian currency dipped to a one-month low of 95.50 per dollar on Wednesday before the Reserve Bank of India intervened with dollar sales, helping it recover to 95.39 by Thursday's close. The broader macro picture is precarious. Market analysts warn that if crude breaches $85 to $90 per barrel, India's current account balance — which had stabilised on the back of diverse sourcing and falling global prices — would come under renewed strain. ## Hormuz at Half Capacity The Strait of Hormuz, which carried roughly a fifth of global oil supplies before the war, is currently operating at about 50 percent of pre-war transit levels, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy. Tehran has maintained that it controls the strait and issues permission to ships on designated routes. The Guards warned that "any further US intervention will draw a crushing response" and that the strait "will be reopened only under Iranian arrangements, not through US threats." For India's 1.3 million citizens working in Gulf states — and for its energy security apparatus — the question is no longer whether the ceasefire holds. It is what comes after it collapses. *Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg via OilPrice.com, Outlook Business, The Hindu BusinessLine, MarketWatch*
